program: Business English for an International Boardroom

lesson.menu_desc: A round of introductions at a global strategy meeting in Tokyo: who you are, what you oversee and what you have been working on lately -- I’ve worked / I’ve been working -- 35 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 1 -- Thirty-Five Years, One Table
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Julius Cesar do Nascimento | Lesson 1 -- Thirty-Five Years, One Table
lesson.grammar_point: present perfect simple (results and totals: I have worked here for 35 years, we have opened two plants) x present perfect continuous (activities still in progress: we have been expanding, I have been traveling a lot)

listenings.text: I'm the purchasing director at a truck manufacturer in Ohio, and I've worked in purchasing for twenty years. In that time, I've visited more than two hundred plants in eleven countries. My job is simple to describe and hard to do: I find suppliers we can trust, and I keep them. For most of my career, our suppliers were in the United States and Mexico. But the last three years have been different. We've been buying more castings from Asia and from Brazil, because prices in Mexico have gone up. So I've been traveling much more than before. I've spent the last two weeks in Japan and Korea. What do I look for in a new supplier? A good track record on quality, and people who answer the phone when there's a problem.

I've been the manager of this plant near Pune for five years. When I arrived, we had one production line and about three hundred people. Since then, we've opened two new lines, and we've hired almost six hundred people. Our revenue has doubled. People ask me what the secret is. Honestly, there's no secret. We've been working very closely with our customers, especially the car makers in the north of India. Every month, I sit down with their engineers and we look at the problems together. Recently we've been testing a new kind of part for electric cars, and it has been the most difficult project of my career. We haven't solved everything yet, but we've learned a lot.

I've sat on the boards of six companies, and I've listened to hundreds of presentations. So here is my advice for anyone who has to introduce themselves in an international meeting. Don't read your CV. Nobody at the table needs every job you've had. Say three things: who you are, what you're responsible for, and what you've been working on lately. The last part is the most important, because it tells us why you're in the room today. And keep it short. Thirty seconds is enough. If you have a strong track record, the numbers will speak for you. Oh, and one more thing. If you don't understand a question, ask. Nobody thinks less of you. We all have accents, and we've all been lost at some point.
